title: Metals, Reactivity and Extraction
strapline: One ordered list that explains corrosion, displacement and why we mine what we mine.
bigIdea: Metals can be placed in a single order of reactivity. That order explains which metals corrode, which displace others, and which method is needed to get a metal out of its ore.
priorKnowledge: Unit 4: displacement reactions and the deduced metal order.
futureLearning: GCSE: electrolysis of molten and aqueous compounds, reduction and oxidation in terms of electrons, life cycle assessment.

misconceptions.misconception: Gold and platinum are valuable because they are rare, not because they are unreactive.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Rarity is the everyday explanation for price.
misconceptions.addressIt: Connect unreactivity to being found native and to not tarnishing; show that copper is common but still used for its low reactivity in plumbing.

misconceptions.misconception: Rusting is just metal getting dirty or wearing away.
misconceptions.addressIt: Run the rusting conditions experiment; show rust is a new substance (iron oxide) with greater mass than the iron consumed.

misconceptions.whyItSticks: Corrode and rust are used interchangeably.
misconceptions.addressIt: Define rusting as specific to iron and steel; use corrosion as the general term and test aluminium and copper for comparison.

misconceptions.misconception: Extraction with carbon works for every metal.
misconceptions.whyItSticks: Pupils learn one method and generalise.
misconceptions.addressIt: Place carbon in the reactivity series explicitly and reason which metals sit above it and therefore need electrolysis.

keyVocabulary.definition: A list of metals in order of how readily they react.
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extraction worthwhile.
Obtaining a metal from its compound.
A reaction in which a substance loses oxygen.
The reaction of a metal with substances in its surroundings, such as oxygen and water.
Using electricity to break down a compound into its elements.

practicals.title: Conditions needed for rusting
hazards: Anhydrous calcium chloride is an irritant
control: Goggles; teacher boils and cools the water in advance
Tubes stored in a rack in a safe corner for one week
practicals.timing: 25 minutes to set up, 10 minutes a week later

practicals.title: Reduction of copper oxide with carbon
hazards: Very hot tube; the mixture glows
control: Teacher demonstration behind a screen; goggles for the front row
Remove the delivery tube from the limewater before stopping heating

practicals.title: Ordering metals by reaction with water and acid
control: Goggles; small pieces and test tube quantities only
No naked flames while hydrogen is being produced

formative: Reactivity series ordering task from experimental evidence, not from memory.

summative.title: Metals and Extraction assessment
summative.style: 25 marks, 35 minutes, including an investigation-design question on rusting.
summative.markSchemeNotes: In the investigation question, credit a named control variable and a stated fair-test reason.

lessons.title: Building the reactivity series
objectives: Order metals by reactivity using experimental evidence
Write word equations for metal reactions
retrieval: Which metal displaced copper in Unit 4?

sequence.detail: Recall of Unit 4 displacement results and Unit 5 acid reactions.
Four metals with water and with dilute acid; record observations and any temperature change.
Construct the order from the evidence; compare with the standard series and account for any differences.
Exit ticket.

keyQuestions: Which evidence is strongest for placing iron?
Why might your order differ from the textbook one?
support: Observation table with a 0-3 vigour scale.
challenge: Design an additional test to separate two metals that behaved similarly.
lessons.homework: Learn the reactivity series with a mnemonic; word equations for four reactions.
lessons.exitTicket: Order magnesium, copper and zinc from most to least reactive.

lessons.title: Corrosion and rusting
objectives: State the conditions needed for rusting
retrieval: State the reactivity series top to bottom
Is rusting a chemical or physical change?

sequence.detail: Reactivity series recall from memory.
Class designs the four-tube experiment; identify independent, dependent and control variables explicitly.
Set up the four tubes and label; predictions recorded in writing.
Word equation for rusting; prevention methods (barrier, galvanising, sacrificial protection) with links to reactivity.
Exit ticket.

keyQuestions: Why does zinc plating still protect iron when the plating is scratched?
support: Variable-identification frame with the independent variable supplied.
challenge: Explain sacrificial protection in terms of the reactivity series.
lessons.homework: Evaluate three rust prevention methods for a named object, such as a bridge.
lessons.exitTicket: Name the two substances needed for rusting.

lessons.title: Ores and extraction with carbon
objectives: Explain why most metals are found as compounds
Relate the method of extraction to position in the reactivity series

sequence.detail: Reactivity series and rusting conditions.
Native metals versus ores; place carbon in the series; carbon reduces oxides of metals below it only.
Copper oxide reduced by carbon; copper colour appears; limewater test confirms carbon dioxide.
For eight named metals, state the extraction method and justify from position.
Exit ticket.

keyQuestions: Why is gold found as the metal itself?
Why can carbon not be used to extract aluminium?
support: Reactivity series with carbon marked on it displayed at every bench.
challenge: Write balanced symbol equations for two reduction reactions.
lessons.homework: Explain why the method of extraction depends on reactivity.
lessons.exitTicket: Name one metal extracted with carbon and one that cannot be.

lessons.title: Electrolysis and the cost of extraction
objectives: Describe electrolysis as a method of extraction

sequence.detail: Extraction method matching, six metals.
Electrolysis explained at KS3 level: electricity splits the compound. Aluminium as the case study, including the energy cost.
Compare energy needed to extract versus recycle aluminium; calculate the percentage saving.
Structured discussion and written judgement on whether recycling is always better.

keyQuestions: Why is aluminium so much more expensive to extract than iron?
What are the drawbacks of recycling?
support: Calculation frame with the percentage formula supplied.
challenge: Research and evaluate biological methods of extraction such as phytomining.
lessons.homework: Six-mark question comparing extraction and recycling of aluminium.
lessons.exitTicket: Give one reason electrolysis is costly.

lessons.title: Rusting results and evaluation
objectives: Interpret the results of the rusting investigation
Evaluate the method and suggest improvements
retrieval: Name the two conditions needed for rusting
What was the control tube for?

sequence.detail: Recall the predictions made a week earlier.
Examine and photograph the four tubes; record observations against predictions.
Write a full conclusion with evidence; identify two weaknesses in the method and propose improvements.
Model a strong evaluation paragraph; pupils improve their own in green pen.

keyQuestions: Does the evidence prove both conditions are needed, or only that both together cause rust?
How could the experiment be made more reliable?
support: Conclusion writing frame with sentence stems.
challenge: Design a follow-up investigation into whether salt water accelerates rusting, with full variable control.
lessons.exitTicket: State one improvement you would make to this method.

lessons.title: Review and assessment

sequence.detail: Reactivity series, extraction methods and rusting conditions from memory.
25-mark assessment.
Whole-class feedback on the investigation-design question.

support: Reactivity series provided in the assessment.
challenge: Write a mark scheme for the investigation question and peer-assess.
lessons.exitTicket: Which part of the reactivity series do you still mix up?
